claims.text: The magnetocaloric response is governed by microstructural modulation of the first-order magnetostructural transition.
Hysteresis is governed by the alloy's grain size and phase distribution.
The as-deposited alloy has a single-phase hexagonal structure.
Annealing below the phase-transformation temperature will induce grain growth.
The proposed annealing will modify phase distribution without changing overall composition.
An inert annealing atmosphere will prevent oxidation.
Annealing-induced microstructural modification reduces internal stresses.
Annealing-induced microstructural modification reduces pinning sites.
Internal stresses and pinning sites contribute to hysteresis.
Grain growth and phase homogenization sharpen the magnetostructural transition.
Sharpening the magnetostructural transition enhances the magnetocaloric effect.
Reducing internal stresses and pinning sites reduces hysteretic losses.
The annealed alloy will have a sharper magnetocaloric transition than the as-deposited alloy.
The annealed alloy will have a larger peak entropy change than the as-deposited alloy.
The annealed alloy will have a smaller hysteresis width than the as-deposited alloy during low-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
The as-deposited baseline has a broad and hysteretic magnetocaloric response.
The predicted effects hold only below the phase-transformation temperature and for durations that do not produce secondary phases or decomposition.

contradictions.description: The initial material is described as single-phase, yet the intervention is supposed to modify and homogenize its phase distribution while avoiding secondary-phase formation. The hypothesis does not identify what nonuniform multiphase distribution exists in the stated single-phase baseline.
